Opportunistic describes someone (or something) that takes advantage of a situation as soon as it arises — not because of careful planning or strong principles, but simply because the chance is there.

Think of it this way: an opportunistic person doesn't create situations. They exploit them the moment they appear, often acting quickly and flexibly, but usually without much concern for fairness, loyalty, or ethics.
The Connotation — Is It a Bad Word?

This depends entirely on the context.

When used to describe human behavior, it almost always carries a negative or suspicious tone. Calling a person opportunistic is rarely a compliment. It implies they are self-serving — that they will bend their values, switch sides, or take advantage of others the moment it benefits them. It suggests a lack of principle.

However, when used in science (biology or medicine), it is completely neutral — just a factual description of a pattern.

This is the most common everyday use.

An opportunistic person watches for openings and exploits them for personal gain, regardless of whether it is the right thing to do, or whether it hurts others. They don't necessarily plan to do wrong — they simply don't let ethics, loyalty, or fairness stop them when an opportunity appears.

Examples:

  • A colleague who takes credit for your idea the moment you present it in a meeting — not because they had a scheme, but because the opening was there — is being opportunistic.
  • A politician who suddenly changes their stated beliefs to match whatever opinion is popular at the time, purely to gain more votes, is acting opportunistically.
  • A friend who is warm and helpful to you only when they need something from you, and distant otherwise, is an opportunistic friend.

The thread connecting all of these is: personal advantage comes first, principles come second (or not at all).
The Key Distinction: Opportunistic vs. Simply Ambitious

This is an important line to draw.

An ambitious person sets goals, works hard, and grabs opportunities — but usually with some code of conduct. They want to succeed, but they care how they succeed.

An opportunistic person, on the other hand, is more reactive and unprincipled. They don't necessarily work toward a goal — they simply pounce the moment a chance appears, with little regard for whether their action is fair, honest, or consistent with what they claimed to believe.

In short: ambition is about drive. Opportunism is about exploitation.

When describing crimes, the word is used in a more neutral, descriptive way — meaning the crime was unplanned.

An opportunistic crime is one where the criminal didn't set out to commit a crime that day. They simply spotted an easy opening and acted on it. For example, someone who notices an unlocked car with a wallet sitting on the seat and steals it — without having planned to steal anything — has committed an opportunistic theft. The situation created the crime, not prior scheming.

This is why it's used in a more neutral tone here — it describes the nature of the act (unplanned, situational), not necessarily a character flaw.

In nature, an opportunistic species or opportunistic feeder is one that is highly adaptable — it doesn't rely on one specific food source or habitat. It eats or lives wherever and whenever resources become available.

A crow is a great example. It doesn't specialize. It eats scraps, insects, grains, carrion — whatever is accessible. It thrives because it is flexible and exploits whatever the environment offers at any given moment.

Here, "opportunistic" is a compliment of sorts — it means resilient and adaptable.

This is a very specific and important use of the word.

An opportunistic infection is one caused by a germ (bacteria, virus, or fungus) that does not normally cause illness in a healthy person — but causes serious disease when the body's immune system is weakened.

These germs are called opportunistic because they "seize the opportunity" created by the body's vulnerability. They cannot overpower a strong immune system, so they wait, essentially, until the defenses are down — then they strike.

This is why patients with HIV/AIDS, or those undergoing chemotherapy (both of which weaken immunity), are especially at risk for opportunistic infections. The same germs that would be harmless to a healthy person become life-threatening to them.
How to Use It in Sentences

• "He was an opportunistic investor — he never had a strategy, he just bought whatever seemed cheap that day."
  • "The robbery was opportunistic — the thief saw an open window and climbed in on impulse."
  • "Her critics accused her of being opportunistic, saying she only supported the cause when it was politically convenient."
  • "Crows are opportunistic feeders that can survive in almost any environment."
  • "The patient developed an opportunistic infection after weeks of chemotherapy."
One-Line Summary to Lock It In

Opportunistic = taking advantage of a situation the moment it appears, driven by self-interest or circumstance rather than planning or principle — a negative quality in people, a neutral or positive trait in nature and science.
